analysis.one_liner: Limits workplace surveillance and employee data collection, and requires employers to disclose what they collect.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors in June 2026 and sent to three House committees; it has received no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar most employers from using electronic surveillance and data collection to monitor workers' union activity, off-duty life, health, politics, immigration status, or whistleblowing. It would require employers to disclose exactly what data they collect on each worker, how, and how it feeds into decisions like firing, discipline, or promotion. Workers could see and correct that data, challenge automated decisions based on it, and sue with attorney's fees if employers violate the rules. A new Worker Protection and Technology Division inside the Labor Department would enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more employees, including contractors performing paid work, federal and congressional employees. The bill's strongest benefits go to people trying to organize a union, report legal violations, or contest an automated firing or performance score: those practices would be explicitly barred, and retaliation against workers exercising these rights would carry damages of $5,000 to $100,000 per violation. Every covered worker would gain the right to see, correct, and challenge the data their boss keeps on them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and job applicants under employer surveillance

how_it_helps.text: Bars employers from collecting or using employee data to identify union organizing, protected concerted activity, political or religious views, unrelated health conditions, immigration status, or whistleblowing, and from monitoring workers off duty in break rooms, locker rooms, lactation spaces, or at home [S2].
Requires employers to disclose what data they collect on each worker, how, how often, who has access, and how it affects decisions like performance reviews, hiring, and firing [S2].

Gives workers the right to obtain their data within 30 days, correct errors, and, when a work-related decision uses their data, review it, fix it, and request reconsideration within at least 7 days [S2].

Prohibits selling worker data and transferring it to third parties, requires opt-in consent plus encryption before any transfer to a service provider, and mandates deletion of applicant and former-employee data after 3 years [S2].

Creates a private right of action with double actual damages, statutory damages from $5,000 to $100,000 depending on the violation, attorney's fees, and invalidates forced arbitration and class-action waivers for these claims [S2].

Establishes a Worker Protection and Technology Division in the Labor Department to investigate and enforce the rules using Fair Labor Standards Act authority, with a study and annual public report to Congress on workplace surveillance [S2].

Extends the same protections to congressional staff, federal employees, and state and tribal government workers, and lets state attorneys general and state privacy regulators sue on residents' behalf [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more employees bear the cost: they would have to inventory and restrict their data collection, publish detailed disclosures, build access and correction systems, and stop or rework surveillance-driven performance management. Vendors of workplace monitoring software, biometric systems, and people-analytics tools lose a market, since employers could only use their products for narrowly permitted, disclosed purposes. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers, and some legitimate productivity and safety monitoring would face new friction.

drawbacks.text: The rules reach nearly all data an employer touches about a worker, including emails, messages, productivity metrics, location, and biometrics, and allow collection only if it is 'strictly necessary' and the 'least invasive means' for a listed purpose, a standard that could force employers to abandon some genuine quality, safety, and performance monitoring and invite litigation over what counts as necessary [S2].

Statutory damages of up to $40,000 per data-minimization violation and $100,000 for retaliation, plus a private right of action, would create significant litigation exposure for employers, including public agencies and nonprofits with 11 or more workers [S2].

The bill sets up a new federal division, several advisory boards, and rulemaking across multiple agencies, which takes time and money and may overlap with existing state privacy laws and FTC, EEOC, and NLRB authority, though the bill explicitly preserves rather than preempts those [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a workforce increasingly tracked by software: workers would learn what is being collected, could fix errors that cost them jobs, and could no longer be monitored for organizing or whistleblowing. The costs are real but mostly fall on employers and their vendors, and the bill tries to soften them by allowing data collection for legitimate job, safety, quality, and legal-compliance purposes and by preserving existing law. The main design risk is the 'strictly necessary / least invasive' standard, which is demanding and likely to be fought in court. On balance it is a worker-protection bill whose costs fall mainly on the entities being regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2026 and referred to three House committees, and so far none of them has taken it up, so it sits waiting with only about six months left in this Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the Stop Spying Bosses Act on June 23, 2026, joined by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici [S1] [S2].
It was referred the same day to three committees: Education and Workforce, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration [S4].
The bill has 9 additional cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The only action in the record is introduction and committee referral; there is no hearing, markup, or vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the outcome preserves the status quo: employers keep unrestricted ability to collect and use worker surveillance data, and monitoring-software and people-analytics vendors keep their market. Workers gain nothing until the bill moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and surveillance-software vendors, for now

for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee member

for.name: 9 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill; no Republicans have

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 9 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; the committees that would move the bill are chaired by Republicans, who have not acted on it [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and people-analytics software vendors
industries.note: Their core product, continuous monitoring of worker communications, keystrokes, location, and biometrics, could only be sold for narrow, disclosed, necessary purposes, and the data could never be sold or moved to third parties. Their business model runs directly against the worker rights the bill creates.

industries.industry: Large employers (11 or more workers) using electronic monitoring
industries.note: They would lose the ability to use surveillance data for productivity scoring, automated discipline, and identifying organizers or whistleblowers, and would carry disclosure, access, deletion, and litigation costs. The employers' cost savings from surveillance often come at workers' expense, which is why the interests are opposed here.

industries.industry: HR data and background-screening service providers
industries.note: They could keep processing worker data under strict contracts with opt-in consent and encryption, but could no longer combine a client's data with other employers' data or sell it. Compliant firms keep the business; data-brokering practices end.

analysis.trajectory: Introduced in the final months of a Congress, with no Republican support and referred to three committees, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote; the standard path for a bill at this stage is to die quietly when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless it is attached to a larger moving vehicle.
